title: South African crime exposure, reporting and perceived safety diverge across households, gender and place
source_unit: Statistics South Africa, Governance, Public Safety and Justice Survey 2025/26: Victims of Crime Release
geography: South Africa; households and individuals aged 16 years and older as defined by GPSJS

observations.period: 2025/26; household crime exposure and police reporting

denominator.unit: South African households in the GPSJS 2025/26 release; survey denominator is not stated in the one-page media release

housebreaking_affected_households.unit: percent of households affected by housebreaking; about 1.08 million households and over 1.5 million incidents

housebreaking_reported.unit: percent of affected households reporting some or all housebreaking incidents to police

home_robbery_affected_households.unit: percent of households affected by home robbery; about 179,000 households

home_robbery_reported.unit: percent of affected households reporting some or all home-robbery incidents to police

observations.method: Statistics South Africa media release summarising the nationally scoped GPSJS 2025/26 victims-of-crime results; household-level incidence and reporting measures are presented as estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The one-page release does not provide the full sample design, item denominators, confidence intervals, reasons for non-reporting, police response, case outcomes, or repeat-contact experience.
observations.subgroup: South African households represented by the GPSJS release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Non-reporting may reflect low perceived benefit, fear, access barriers, prior experience, or incident severity; reported cases should not be read as the complete crime burden.

observations.period: 2025/26; individual crime exposure and police reporting

denominator.unit: South African individuals aged 16 years and older in the GPSJS release; survey denominator is not stated in the one-page media release

personal_property_theft_affected.unit: percent of people aged 16+ affected by theft of personal property; about 1.2 million people and 1.4 million incidents

personal_property_theft_reported.unit: percent of affected individuals reporting some or all theft incidents to police

street_robbery_reported.unit: percent of individuals experiencing street robbery reporting some or all incidents to police; about 459,000 individuals

assault_affected_change.value: 408,000 individuals experienced assault in 2025/26, up from 363,000 in 2024/25

observations.method: Statistics South Africa GPSJS 2025/26 victims-of-crime release, with estimated affected individuals and self-reported police reporting.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not establish causal change, incident verification, severity-adjusted reporting, police response, prosecution, recovery, or safety after reporting.
observations.subgroup: Individuals aged 16 years and older represented in the GPSJS release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Changes in reported incidence may reflect recall, survey coverage, classification or reporting changes as well as underlying exposure.

denominator.unit: South African individuals aged 16 years and older in the GPSJS release; item bases are not stated in the one-page media release

safe_day.unit: percent feeling safe walking alone in their neighbourhood during the day

safe_dark.unit: percent feeling safe walking alone in their neighbourhood when it is dark

female_very_unsafe_dark.unit: percent of females reporting feeling very unsafe walking alone after dark; compared with 38.8% of males

female_assault_known_person.unit: percent of females experiencing assault reporting a known person as the perpetrator

observations.method: GPSJS 2025/26 self-reported safety and assault-perpetrator indicators as summarised by Statistics South Africa.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived safety is not observed victimisation or objective risk; the release does not provide subgroup denominators, confidence intervals, place-level causal explanations, or service outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Individuals aged 16 years and older, with gender-specific results for perceived safety and assault context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower perceived safety can reflect visibility, social norms, prior experience or media attention, not only current incidence; known-person assault does not by itself identify prevention or remedy needs.

denominator.unit: South African individuals aged 16 years and older in the GPSJS release; item base is not stated in the one-page media release

self_protection_action.unit: percent reporting that they had done something to protect themselves against crime

security_conversion.value: crime exposure and perceived insecurity are converted into household and individual protective action, while formal reporting remains partial

observations.method: GPSJS 2025/26 comparison of self-reported protective behaviour with the prior reporting period.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not identify the protective acts, their cost, effectiveness, unequal burden, or whether they improve safety, mobility, trust or reporting.
observations.subgroup: Individuals aged 16 years and older represented in the GPSJS release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Protective action may be precautionary rather than a response to direct victimisation, and may include low-cost behaviour changes as well as substantial household expense.

related_sources.claim: Statistics South Africa crime publication hub and related GPSJS context.

boundary: This record adds a public-safety conversion mechanism: victimisation, police reporting, perceived safety and self-protection are distinct stages, with gender and place shaping usable security. The one-page official release does not establish objective crime prevalence, reporting causes, police remedy, protection effectiveness, household cost, or causal change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The Statistics South Africa GPSJS 2025/26 Victims of Crime media release was reviewed for household and individual crime incidence, reporting, perceived safety, gendered assault context and self-protection comparisons.
